Degenerate Cahn-Hilliard systems: From nonlocal to local

José A. Carrillo Address: José A. Carrillo: Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Woodstock Road, Oxford, OX2 6GG, United Kingdom Email address: carrillo@maths.ox.ac.uk , Charles Elbar Address: Charles Elbar: Sorbonne Université, Laboratoire Jacques-Louis Lions (LJLL), F-75005 Paris, France Email address: charles.elbar@sorbonne-universite.fr and Jakub Skrzeczkowski Address: Jakub Skrzeczkowski: Institute of Mathematics of Polish Academy of Sciences; Faculty of Mathematics, Informatics and Mechanics, University of Warsaw, Poland Email address: jakub.skrzeczkowski@student.uw.edu.pl
Abstract.

We provide a rigorous mathematical framework to establish the limit of a nonlocal model of cell-cell adhesion system to a local model. When the parameter of the nonlocality goes to 0, the system tends to a Cahn-Hilliard system with degenerate mobility and cross interaction forces. Our analysis relies on a priori estimates and compactness properties.

Key words and phrases: 
Degenerate Cahn-Hilliard equation; Nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation; Aggregation-Diffusion; Singular limit
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B40, 35D30, 35K25, 35K55

1. Introduction

We consider the nonlocal system of Cahn-Hilliard equation with degenerate mobility derived in [35]

Here κ,α,γ>0\kappa,\alpha,\gamma>0, β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} while BB is the nonlocal operator B=BεB=B_{\varepsilon} defined with

Our target is to prove that as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the constructed solutions of

∂ρ∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} =∇⋅(ρ∇(κBε[ρ]+αBε[η]−γρ−βη)),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho\nabla\left(\kappa B_{\varepsilon}[\rho]+\alpha B_{\varepsilon}[\eta]-\gamma\rho-\beta\eta\right)\right), in(0,+∞)×𝕋d,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}, (1.5)

∂ρ∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} =∇⋅(ρ∇(−κΔρ−αΔη−γρ−βη)),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(\rho\nabla\left(-\kappa\Delta\rho-\alpha\Delta\eta-\gamma\rho-\beta\eta\right)\right), (1.7)

It turns out (see Proposition 2.1) that for κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2}, κ>0\kappa>0 they provide strong compactness in space of ρε\rho_{\varepsilon}, ηε\eta_{\varepsilon}, ∇ρε\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}, ∇ηε\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}.

Our first result states that we can construct solutions to (1.5)-(1.6) satisfying additional uniform estimates which will be relevant in the sequel.

Theorem 1.1 (Existence of solutions for the nonlocal system).

Suppose that κ>0\kappa>0, κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2}. Let ε0=min⁡(ε0A,ε0B)\varepsilon_{0}=\min(\varepsilon_{0}^{A},\varepsilon_{0}^{B}) be given by Proposition 2.1 and Lemma 3.2. Let u0=(ρ0,η0)∈𝒫​(𝕋d)2u_{0}=(\rho_{0},\eta_{0})\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{T}^{d})^{2} be an initial datum with finite energy and entropy Eε​(u0),Φ⁡(u0)≤CE_{\varepsilon}(u^{0}),\Phi(u^{0})\leq C defined in  (1.9)-(1.10) where CC is independent of ε\varepsilon. Let ε≤ε0\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0}. Then, there exists a global weak solution uε∈𝒫​(𝕋d)2u_{\varepsilon}\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{T}^{d})^{2} of (1.5)-(1.6) as defined in Definition 3.1. Moreover, it satisfies

∫𝕋d∫𝕋dωε​(y)ε2​(|ρε​(x)−ρε​(x−y)|2+|ηε​(x)−ηε​(x−y)|2)​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑y≤C,\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{\omega_{\varepsilon}(y)}{\varepsilon^{2}}(|\rho_{\varepsilon}(x)-\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)|^{2}+|\eta_{\varepsilon}(x)-\eta_{\varepsilon}(x-y)|^{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq C, (1.13)
∫0T∫𝕋d∫𝕋dωε​(y)ε2​(|∇ρε​(x)−∇ρε​(x−y)|2+|∇ηε​(x)−∇ηε​(x−y)|2)​⁡d​x​⁡d​y​⁡𝑑t≤C,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{\omega_{\varepsilon}(y)}{\varepsilon^{2}}(|\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(x)-\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)|^{2}+|\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}(x)-\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}(x-y)|^{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq C, (1.14)

for a constant CC that depends on parameters and the initial condition u0u^{0} but not on ε\varepsilon.

The proof of this result follows the argument of [29]. We decided to include the proof to demonstrate estimates (1.13)–(1.14) which are essential for our main result which reads as follows.

Theorem 1.2 (Convergence of nonlocal to local Cahn-Hilliard equation on the torus).

Suppose that κ>0\kappa>0, κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2}. Let u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 be an initial datum with finite energy and entropy Eε​(u0),Φ⁡(u0)≤CE_{\varepsilon}(u^{0}),\Phi(u^{0})\leq C defined in  (1.9) and (1.10) where CC is independent of ε\varepsilon. Let {uε}\{u_{\varepsilon}\} be a sequence of solutions of the degenerate nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation (1.5)-(1.6) as defined in Definition 3.1. Then, up to a subsequence (not relabelled),

uε→u​ in ​L2​(0,T,H1​(𝕋d)),u_{\varepsilon}\to u\mbox{ in }L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))\,,

where uu is a weak solution of the degenerate Cahn-Hilliard system (1.7)-(1.8) as in Definition 4.1.

We conclude with a short discussion of applied techniques and considered problems.

Existence of weak solutions. The strategy to prove the existence of weak solutions is based on the gradient flow structure of the equation in the Wasserstein space. We use the JKO scheme first introduced in [41] by Jordan, Kinderlehrer and Otto in the context of the Fokker-Planck equation. The main idea is to use an implicit time discretization of the associated variational problems. The sequence created minimizes movements. When the time step goes to 0, the sequence converges to the associated gradient flow. This strategy has been used for instance in [43, 42] in the context of Cahn-Hilliard equation and in [29] in the context of cross-diffusion systems with nonlocal interaction. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is in fact closely related to the one in [29] and we follow to some extent their proof. The difference is the control of the positiveness of the energy and the transport of uniform bounds independently of ε\varepsilon needed in the last section. Also, our settings are periodic in space. The proof uses two main components:

  • •

    The "gradient flow" structure of the scheme which provides classical discrete energy estimates and Hölder continuity in time and allow narrow convergences of the scheme.

  • •

    The weak convergences being not enough, we use the flow interchange lemma [44, 43]. The idea is that we usually obtain better estimates with the entropy in the Cahn-Hilliard equation. This entropy generates a heat-flow. Then the flow interchange lemma allows to exchange the dissipation of one functional along the gradient flow of another one and thus improve the regularity of the scheme.

Nevertheless, since we assume that κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2} and κ>0\kappa>0, the system is strongly parabolic with respect to (ρ,η)(\rho,\eta). Therefore, to prove existence, one could approximate (1.5)–(1.6) by

∂ρ∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} =∇⋅(Tδ(ρ)∇(κBε[ρ]+αBε[η]−γρ−βη)),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(T_{\delta}(\rho)\nabla\left(\kappa B_{\varepsilon}[\rho]+\alpha B_{\varepsilon}[\eta]-\gamma\rho-\beta\eta\right)\right), in(0,+∞)×𝕋d,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}, (1.15)
∂η∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t} =∇⋅(Tδ(η)∇(αBε[ρ]+Bε[η]−βρ−η)),\displaystyle=\nabla\cdot\left(T_{\delta}(\eta)\nabla\left(\alpha B_{\varepsilon}[\rho]+B_{\varepsilon}[\eta]-\beta\rho-\eta\right)\right), in(0,+∞)×𝕋d,\displaystyle\text{in}\quad(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}, (1.16)

where TδT_{\delta} is a function such that δ≤Tδ≤1δ\delta\leq T_{\delta}\leq\frac{1}{\delta} and Tδ​(ϱ)→ϱT_{\delta}(\varrho)\to\varrho as δ→0\delta\to 0. Then, one sends δ→0\delta\to 0 and obtains solutions to (1.5)–(1.6). This method is a standard way of proving existence of solutions to Cahn-Hilliard equation with degenerate mobility [28, 33, 31, 47]. Of course, one has to prove estistence to (1.15)–(1.16) by virtue of fixed point method and Schauder’s estimates for parabolic equations which is very technical. Therefore, we preferred to apply gradient flow techniques which are natural for our problem.

Passage to the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and nonlocal compactness results. We use the strategy developed by the second and third author in [32] for the single Cahn-Hilliard equation. The main tool is the compactness result due to Bourgain-Brezis-Mironescu [11] and Ponce [48] which reads as follows:

Proposition 1.3.

Let {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} be a sequence bounded in L2​(𝕋d)L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}). Suppose that

∫𝕋d∫𝕋d|fε​(x)−fε​(y)|2|x−y|2​ωε​(|x−y|)​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑y≤C\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{|f_{\varepsilon}(x)-f_{\varepsilon}(y)|^{2}}{|x-y|^{2}}\omega_{\varepsilon}(|x-y|)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq C (1.17)

for some constant CC. Then, {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} is strongly compact in L2​(𝕋d)L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) and the limit f∈W1,2​(𝕋d)f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}).

Proposition 1.3 is crucial because the difference quotient appearing in (1.17) can be controlled by the energy and the dissipation of the entropy of Cahn-Hilliard equation which yields compactness. The novelty in this paper comes from the treating of cross-interactions terms. It turns out that we can control possibly negative terms appearing in the energy and the dissipation of entropy by a simple interpolation inequality, see Lemma 2.2 and Proposition 2.1.

Aggregation-diffusion systems. System (1.5)-(1.6) is an example of aggregation-diffusion system [18] which are attracting a lot of mathematical attention nowadays [51, 21, 6, 22, 34]. To motivate, let us first start with an aggregation equation

∂ρ∂t+∇⋅(ρu)=0,u=−∇W∗ρ,\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot(\rho u)=0,\qquad u=-\nabla W\ast\rho, (1.18)

where W:𝕋d→ℝW:\mathbb{T}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is a symmetric interaction potential. Over the last years, equation (1.18) was applied in the context of biological aggregation [10, 52, 46], materials science [38], granular media [24, 7] and it attracted also a lot of mathematical interest, particularly for non-smooth potentials. We only refer to [9] for the LpL^{p} theory, to [19] for the theory in spaces of measures and to [8] for blow-up conditions. Equation (1.18) can be derived from the particle system via mean-field limit [40, 39]: one considers NN particles having positions {Xi}i=1,…,N\{X_{i}\}_{i=1,...,N} satisfying system of ODEs:

Xi′=−1N∑j≠i∇W(Xi−Xj);X_{i}^{\prime}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\neq i}\nabla W(X_{i}-X_{j});

then, under appropriate assumptions on WW, empirical measure ρN​(t)=1N​∑i=1NδXi​(t)\rho^{N}(t)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{X_{i}(t)} converges (in the weak∗ topology of measures) to a solution of (1.18), see [15, Theorem 3.1] for the proof and [16] for some extensions.

To obtain the aggregation-diffusion equation from (1.18), one can consider interaction potentials of the form Wν=W+2​ν​δ0W_{\nu}=W+2\nu\delta_{0} modeling two effects: repulsion of strength ν\nu and non-local attraction. Informally, we obtain

∂ρ∂t=νΔρ2+∇⋅(ρ∇W∗ρ),\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}=\nu\,\Delta\rho^{2}+\nabla\cdot(\rho\,\nabla W\ast\rho), (1.19)

but this can be made rigorous by approximating the Dirac mass with a sequence of mollifiers, see [17, 12] with m=2m=2. Of course, (1.19) can be extended to include more general diffusion term Δ​ρm\Delta\rho^{m} instead of Δ​ρ2\Delta\rho^{2} as well as an advection term, see [20].

One can also consider system of particles {Xi}i=1,…,N\{X_{i}\}_{i=1,...,N}, {Yi}i=1,…,N\{Y_{i}\}_{i=1,...,N} representing two populations. Then, repeating the derivation explained above, one arrives at a system of equations of the form (1.1)–(1.2) which can be used to model cell-cell adhesion [2, 23, 25] to reproduce the Steinberg cell-sorting phenomena. Structure preserving numerical schemes have been derived for equations and systems of aggregation-diffusion type [14, 3, 4] as well as Cahn-Hilliard equations and systems [5, 35] recovering the cell sorting mechanism.

Gradient flows in the periodic setting. Due to the presence of a non-local operator BεB_{\varepsilon} in (1.5)–(1.6), we develop our theory on the dd-dimensional torus 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} which makes non-local terms easy to be defined. As already explained, solutions to (1.5)–(1.6) will be constructed via JKO scheme. In what follows, we briefly review the theory of optimal transport on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} comparing to the usual case of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} or bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. We refer the Reader to [50, Section 1.3.2].

First, we need to define a metric and the natural choice is

d⁡(x,y)=infk∈ℤd|x−y+k|,x,y∈𝕋d,d(x,y)=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}|x-y+k|,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb{T}^{d},

where |⋅||\cdot| is the Euclidean distance. Then, the Wasserstein distance W2{W}_{2} is defined as

W22​(μ,ν)=infπ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)∫𝕋d×𝕋dd​(x,y)2​⁡d​π​(x,y),μ,ν∈𝒫⁡(𝕋d),{W}_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}}d(x,y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi(x,y),\qquad\mu,\nu\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{T}^{d}),

where Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) is the set of couplings between μ\mu and ν\nu. This already implies that, say in dimension d=1d=1, the optimal transport maps are not necessarily monotone on the torus. Nevertheless, the optimal map always exists if at least one of the measures is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebegue measure. Moreover, the optimal map is given by the gradient of some function which is differentiable a.e. We refer to [27] for the first proof of this fact and to [50, Theorem 1.25] for a modern presentation. We also refer to the general result of McCann [45] who proved existence of the optimal map on the general manifold, including the case of torus.

To conclude, let us mention that optimal transport was used to study several PDEs on the torus via JKO scheme, in particular fractional porous medium equation [36], continuity equation with nonlocal velocity in 1D [37], systems of continuity equations with nonlinear diffusion and nonlocal drifts [13] and certain fourth-order equation in one dimension [26].

2. Energy and entropy for the non-local system

As already mentioned, system (1.5)–(1.6) has the energy/entropy structure which can be used to obtain compactness estimates. In order to do so, one has to assure nonnegativity of the quantities of interest. In our case, we focus on the energy EεE_{\varepsilon} and the dissipation of entropy 𝒟​Φ\mathcal{D}\Phi.

Proposition 2.1.

Suppose that κ>0\kappa>0, κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2}. Then, there exists ε0A>0\varepsilon_{0}^{A}>0 depending on κ\kappa, α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma with the following property: for all ε∈(0,ε0A)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}^{A}) and ρ,η∈𝒫⁡(𝕋d)\rho,\eta\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{T}^{d}), up to a constant, the energy defined by (1.9) and the dissipation of the entropy defined in (1.12) are nonnegative and provide the estimates on the quantities

∫𝕋d∫𝕋dωε​(y)ε2​(|ρ⁡(x)−ρ⁡(x−y)|2+|η⁡(x)−η⁡(x−y)|2)​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑y≤C+Eε​[ρ,η],\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{\omega_{\varepsilon}(y)}{\varepsilon^{2}}(|\rho(x)-\rho(x-y)|^{2}+|\eta(x)-\eta(x-y)|^{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq C+E_{\varepsilon}[\rho,\eta],
∫0t∫𝕋d∫𝕋dωε​(y)ε2​(|∇ρ​(x)−∇ρ​(x−y)|2+|∇η​(x)−∇η​(x−y)|2)​⁡d​x​⁡d​y​⁡𝑑s≤C+𝒟​Φ​[ρ,η]​(t),\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{\omega_{\varepsilon}(y)}{\varepsilon^{2}}(|\nabla\rho(x)-\nabla\rho(x-y)|^{2}+|\nabla\eta(x)-\nabla\eta(x-y)|^{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\leq C+\mathcal{D}\Phi[\rho,\eta](t),

where CC depends on κ\kappa, α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma.

The main tool to establish nonnegativity (up to a constant) is the following non-local Poincare inequality with parameter which allows to handle negative terms.

Lemma 2.2 (Poincare inequality with a parameter).

Suppose that κ>0\kappa>0, κ>α2\kappa>\alpha^{2}. 3.2. H1H^{1} estimates for the JKO scheme via flow interchange lemma

The weak convergence of the JKO scheme is not enough to pass to the limit in the definition of weak solutions. We need to obtain better estimates on the solutions. In the Cahn-Hilliard equation, better estimates are derived from considering the functional 𝒰⁡[ρ,η]=∫ρ​log⁡ρ+η​log⁡η\mathcal{U}[\rho,\eta]=\int\rho\log\rho+\eta\log\eta. This functional generates the heat flow with respect to the Wasserstein distance 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2}. To improve the regularity we, therefore, use the flow interchange lemma which states that the dissipation of one functional along the gradient flow of another functional equals the dissipation of the second functional along the gradient flow of the first one.

The main result of this section reads:

Proposition 3.5.

Each solution of the JKO scheme (3.5) satisfies

uτn∈H1​(𝕋d)for all n∈ℕ, τ>0u_{\tau}^{n}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})\quad\text{for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\tau>0$}

and the time-interpolation uτ=(ρτ,ητ)u_{\tau}=(\rho_{\tau},\eta_{\tau}) satisfies

∫0T∫𝕋d∫𝕋dωε​(y)ε2​(|∇ρτ​(t,x)−∇ρτ​(t,x−y)|2+|∇ητ​(t,x)−∇ητ​(t,x−y)|2)​⁡d​x​⁡d​y​⁡𝑑t≤C​T,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{\omega_{\varepsilon}(y)}{\varepsilon^{2}}(|\nabla\rho_{\tau}(t,x)-\nabla\rho_{\tau}(t,x-y)|^{2}+|\nabla\eta_{\tau}(t,x)-\nabla\eta_{\tau}(t,x-y)|^{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq CT,

for all T>0T>0. Moreover, for every sequence τk↓0\tau_{k}\downarrow 0, we can extract a subsequence (still denoted by τk\tau_{k}) such that for all T>0T>0,

uτk\displaystyle u_{\tau_{k}} →u​ strongly in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)\displaystyle\to u\text{ strongly in $L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d})$}
uτk\displaystyle u_{\tau_{k}} ⇀u​ weakly in L2​(0,T,H1​(𝕋d)).\displaystyle\rightharpoonup u\text{ weakly in $L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$}.

3.3. Weak formulation

To derive the weak formulation, we follow [53, Section 8.4.2]. Since (3.5) was derived from the Lagrangian point of view, the idea is to investigate its first variation and prove that it is a time-discrete scheme of (3.1). For this, we introduce a suitable perturbation of uτn+1=(ρτn+1,ητn+1)u_{\tau}^{n+1}=(\rho_{\tau}^{n+1},\eta_{\tau}^{n+1}) as follows: let ξ\xi be a smooth periodic vector field and Tδ=Id+δ​ξT_{\delta}=\Id+\delta\xi. It is classical to prove that for δ\delta small enough, TδT_{\delta} is a C1C^{1} diffeomorphism and det(∇Tδ)>0\det(\nabla T_{\delta})>0. Then, we define

u~δ=(Tδ​#​ρτn+1,ητn+1).\tilde{u}_{\delta}=(T_{\delta}\#\rho_{\tau}^{n+1},\eta_{\tau}^{n+1}).

Note carefully that only the first component was perturbed. This will result in the first equation in Definition 3.1. To obtain the second one, it is sufficient to introduce a similar perturbation on the second component of uτn+1u_{\tau}^{n+1}. This results in analogous computations as outlined below and we do not repeat them.

    ⟨Bε​[u]​(⋅),φ⁡(⋅)⟩L2​(𝕋d)=⟨Sε​[u]​(⋅,⋅),Sε​[φ]​(⋅,⋅)⟩L2​(𝕋d×𝕋d).\langle B_{\varepsilon}[u](\cdot),\varphi(\cdot)\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}=\langle S_{\varepsilon}[u](\cdot,\cdot),S_{\varepsilon}[\varphi](\cdot,\cdot)\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d})}.
  4. (S4)

    if {uε}\{u_{\varepsilon}\} is strongly compact in L2​(0,T,H1​(𝕋d))L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})) and φ∈L∞​((0,T)×𝕋d)\varphi\in L^{\infty}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}) we have

    ∫0T∫𝕋d∫𝕋d(Sε​[uε])2​φ​(t,x)→∫0T∫𝕋d|∇u​(t,x)|2​φ​(t,x).\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}(S_{\varepsilon}[u_{\varepsilon}])^{2}\,\varphi(t,x)\to\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|\nabla u(t,x)|^{2}\,\varphi(t,x).

4.1. Uniform estimates in ε\varepsilon and compactness

We collect here estimates for the solutions of (1.5)–(1.6) which are uniform in ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Lemma 4.3.

Let (ρε,ηε)(\rho_{\varepsilon},\eta_{\varepsilon}) be the solution of (1.5)–(1.6) constructed in Theorem 1.1. Then, the following sequences are bounded:

  1. (1)

    {ρε}\{\rho_{\varepsilon}\}, {ηε}\{\eta_{\varepsilon}\} in L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω))L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)) and L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)),

  2. (2)

    {∂tρε}\{\partial_{t}\rho_{\varepsilon}\}, {∂tηε}\{\partial_{t}\eta_{\varepsilon}\} in L2​(0,T,H−2−d2​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2-\frac{d}{2}}(\Omega)).

Moreover, the sequences {ρε}\{\rho_{\varepsilon}\}, {ηε}\{\eta_{\varepsilon}\} are strongly compact in L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)) and the limits belong to L2​(0,T,H2​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}(\Omega)).

Remark 4.4.

We note that we cannot use estimates coming from dissipation of the energy (1.11) which can provide better estimates on time derivatives because this information is lost in the JKO scheme. We proceed with a different approach.

Proof of Lemma 4.3.

The first estimate follows from (1.13)–(1.14) and Lemma 2.2. To see the second, we consider equation for ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} and test it with a smooth and compactly supported function φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x). We need to control the following terms

∫0T∫𝕋dρε∇Bε[ρε]⋅∇φdxdt,∫0T∫𝕋dρε∇Bε[ηε]⋅∇φdxdt,∫0T∫𝕋dρε(γ∇ρε−β∇ηε)⋅∇φdxdt.\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\rho_{\varepsilon}\,\nabla B_{\varepsilon}[\rho_{\varepsilon}]\cdot\nabla\varphi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t,\quad\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\rho_{\varepsilon}\,\nabla B_{\varepsilon}[\eta_{\varepsilon}]\cdot\nabla\varphi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t,\quad\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\rho_{\varepsilon}(\gamma\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}-\beta\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon})\cdot\nabla\varphi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

The first two terms are controlled in the same way so that we focus on the second. Using (S3) in Lemma 4.2 and ∇Bε​[ηε]=Bε​[∇ηε]\nabla B_{\varepsilon}[\eta_{\varepsilon}]=B_{\varepsilon}[\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}] we have

∫0T∫𝕋dρε∇Bε[ηε]⋅∇φdxdt=∫0T∫𝕋d∫𝕋dSε[∇ηε]⋅Sε[ρε∇φ]dydxdt\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\rho_{\varepsilon}\,\nabla B_{\varepsilon}[\eta_{\varepsilon}]\cdot\nabla\varphi\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}S_{\varepsilon}[\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}]\cdot S_{\varepsilon}[\rho_{\varepsilon}\,\nabla\varphi]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t

which is bounded if φ∈L2​(0,T,H2​(𝕋d))\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d})). Concerning the third term, it is controlled when ∇φ∈L2​(0,T,L∞​(𝕋d))\nabla\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d})) which is implied by φ∈L2​(0,T,H2+d2​(𝕋d))\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{2+\frac{d}{2}}(\mathbb{T}^{d})) by Sobolev embedding. The conclusion follows.

The strong compactness follows from Lemma B.3 and estimates (1.13)–(1.14).

∎

Appendix A Results on difference quotients

Lemma A.1.

Let {uε}\{u_{\varepsilon}\} be a sequence strongly compact in L2​(0,T,H1​(𝕋d))L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})). Then, for fixed y∈𝕋dy\in\mathbb{T}^{d},

uε​(t,x−ε​y)−uε​(t,x)ε→−∇u(t,x)⋅y strongly in L2((0,T)×𝕋d×𝕋d).\frac{u_{\varepsilon}(t,x-\varepsilon y)-u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)}{\varepsilon}\to-\nabla u(t,x)\cdot y\mbox{ strongly in }L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}).
Proof.

Clearly, the sequence converges in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}), that is

∫0T∫𝕋d|uε​(t,x−ε​y)−uε​(t,x)ε−∇u​(t,x)⋅y|2​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t→0.\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\left|\frac{u_{\varepsilon}(t,x-\varepsilon y)-u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)}{\varepsilon}-\nabla u(t,x)\cdot y\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\to 0.

To see the convergence in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}), it is sufficient to apply dominated convergence theorem as we have the estimate

∫0T∫𝕋d|uε​(t,x−ε​y)−uε​(t,x)ε|2≤∫0T∫𝕋d|∇uε⋅y|2dxdt≤|y|supε∥∇uε∥Lt,x22.\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\left|\frac{u_{\varepsilon}(t,x-\varepsilon y)-u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)}{\varepsilon}\right|^{2}\leq\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\left|\nabla u^{\varepsilon}\cdot y\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq|y|\,\sup_{\varepsilon}\|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}.

∎

Lemma A.2.

Let φ∈L∞​(𝕋d)\varphi\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) and {ηε}\{\eta_{\varepsilon}\} be a sequence such that

    φ⁡(y)​∇ηε​(x)−∇ηε​(x−ε​y)ε\varphi(y)\,\frac{\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}(x)-\nabla\eta_{\varepsilon}(x-\varepsilon y)}{\varepsilon} is bounded in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}),

Appendix B Compactness results

B.1. A version of Lions-Aubin for JKO scheme.

We recall here from [29, Theorem 2.1] a version of Lions-Aubin lemma useful for establishing compactness of a sequence of solutions to JKO scheme. For the proof we refer to [49, Theorem 2].

Theorem B.1.

Let (X,∥⋅∥X)(X,\|\cdot\|_{X}) be a Banach space. We consider

  • •

    a lower semi-continuous functional ℱ:X→[0,+∞]\mathcal{F}:X\to[0,+\infty] with relatively compact sublevels in XX,

  • •

    a pseudo-distance g:X×X→[0,+∞]g:X\times X\to[0,+\infty], that is gg is lower semicontinuous and g⁡(ρ,η)=0g(\rho,\eta)=0 for some ρ,η∈X\rho,\eta\in X such that ℱ⁡(ρ),ℱ⁡(η)<∞\mathcal{F}(\rho),\mathcal{F}(\eta)<\infty implies ρ=η\rho=\eta.

Let UU be a set of measurable functions u:(0,T)×Xu:(0,T)\times X with T>0T>0 fixed. Assume further that

supu∈U∫0Tℱ⁡(u⁡(t))​⁡𝑑t<∞,limh→0supu∈Ug⁡(u⁡(t+h),u⁡(t))​⁡𝑑t=0.\sup_{u\in U}\int_{0}^{T}\mathcal{F}(u(t))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t<\infty,\qquad\lim_{h\to 0}\sup_{u\in U}g(u(t+h),u(t))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=0. (B.1)

Then, UU contains a sequence {un}\{u_{n}\} converging in measure to some u∈Xu\in X, i.e.

∀ε>0|{t∈[0,T]:‖un−u‖X>ε}|→0​ as ​n→∞.\forall_{\varepsilon>0}\left|\{t\in[0,T]:\|u_{n}-u\|_{X}>\varepsilon\}\right|\to 0\mbox{ as }n\to\infty.

In particular, there exists a subsequence (not relabelled) such that

un​(t)→u⁡(t)​ in ​X​ for a.e. ​t∈[0,T].u_{n}(t)\to u(t)\mbox{ in }X\mbox{ for a.e. }t\in[0,T].

B.2. Nonlocal version of Lions-Aubin lemma

The following result was proved in [32, Theorem B.1] based on [11] and [48]. In fact, the proof of Theorem B.2 is the proof of Proposition 1.3 integrated in time.

Theorem B.2.

Let d≥2d\geq 2. Let {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} be a sequence bounded in Lp​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{p}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}). Suppose that there exists a sequence {ρε}\{\rho_{\varepsilon}\} as above such that

∫0T∫𝕋d∫𝕋d|fε​(t,x)−fε​(t,y)|pεp​ωε​(|x−y|)​⁡d​x​⁡d​y​⁡𝑑t≤C\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{|f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,y)|^{p}}{\varepsilon^{p}}\omega_{\varepsilon}(|x-y|)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq C (B.2)

for some constant CC. Then, {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} is compact in space in Lp​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{p}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}), i.e.

limδ→0lim supε→0∫0T∫𝕋d|fε∗φδ​(t,x)−fε​(t,x)|p​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t=0\lim_{\delta\to 0}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}\ast\varphi_{\delta}(t,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{p}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=0 (B.3)

for all families of mollifiers {φδ}0<δ<1\{\varphi_{\delta}\}_{0<\delta<1}.

We prove here:

Suppose that {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} is a sequence bounded in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}) such that

    {∂tfε}\{\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}\} is uniformly bounded in L2​(0,T,H−k​(𝕋d))L^{2}(0,T;H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})) for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},

    {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} is compact in space in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}), i.e.

    limδ→0lim supε→0∫0T∫𝕋d|fε∗φδ​(t,x)−fε​(t,x)|2​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t=0\lim_{\delta\to 0}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}\ast\varphi_{\delta}(t,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=0 (B.4)

    for some family of mollifiers {φδ}0<δ<1\{\varphi_{\delta}\}_{0<\delta<1}.

Then, {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} is compact in time in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}), i.e.

limh→0lim supε→0∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε​(t+h,x)−fε​(t,x)|2​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t→0​ as ​h→0\lim_{h\to 0}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\to 0\mbox{ as }h\to 0 (B.5)

and so, it is compact in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}).

Proof.

Using the mollifiers with δ=δ⁡(h)\delta=\delta(h) depending on hh to be specified later in the way that δ⁡(h)→0\delta(h)\to 0 as h→0h\to 0, we first split

∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε(t+h,x)−fε(t,x)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,x) |2dxdt≤4∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε(t,x)−fε(t,⋅)∗φδ(x)|2dxdt\displaystyle|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq 4\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t
+4∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε(t+h,x)−fε(t+h,⋅)∗φδ(x)|2dxdt\displaystyle+4\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t
+4∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε(t+h,⋅)∗φδ(x)−fε(t,⋅)∗φδ(x)|2dxdt.\displaystyle+4\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

When we apply limit limh→0lim supε→0\lim_{h\to 0}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}, the first and second term vanish due to (B.4). It remains to study the third term. For this, suppose first that fε​(t,⋅)f_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot) is smooth in the time variable. Then,

∫0T−h\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T-h} ∫𝕋d|fε(t+h,⋅)∗φδ(x)−fε(t,⋅)∗φδ(x)|2dxdt=∫0T−h∫𝕋d|∫tt+h∂tfε(s,⋅)∗φδ(x)ds|2dxdt.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\left|\int_{t}^{t+h}\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

Now, we can estimate the convolution as follows

∂tfε(s,⋅)∗φδ(x)=∫𝕋d∂tfε(s,y)φδ(x−y)dy≤∥∂tfε(s,⋅)∥H−k​(𝕋d)∥φδ(x−⋅)∥Hk​(𝕋d).\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,y)\,\varphi_{\delta}(x-y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y\leq\|\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\|_{H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\,\|\varphi_{\delta}(x-\cdot)\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}.

Using this and applying invariance in space of the Hk​(𝕋d)H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) norm we obtain

∫0T−h∫𝕋d|∫tt+h∂tfε(s,⋅)∗φδ(x)ds|2dxdt=h2∥φδ∥Hk​(𝕋d)∫0T−h|1h∫tt+h∥∂tfε(s,⋅)∥H−k​(𝕋d)ds|2dt.\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\left|\int_{t}^{t+h}\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=h^{2}\,\|\varphi_{\delta}\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\int_{0}^{T-h}\left|\frac{1}{h}\int_{t}^{t+h}\|\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\|_{H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

Applying Jensen’s inequality we obtain

h2​‖φδ‖Hk​(𝕋d)​∫0T−h|1h​∫tt+h‖∂tfε​(s,⋅)‖H−k​(𝕋d)​⁡𝑑s|2​⁡𝑑t≤T​h​‖φδ‖Hk​(𝕋d)​‖∂tfε​(s,⋅)‖L2​(0,T,H−k​(𝕋d))2.h^{2}\,\|\varphi_{\delta}\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\int_{0}^{T-h}\left|\frac{1}{h}\int_{t}^{t+h}\|\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\|_{H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s\right|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq Th\,\|\varphi_{\delta}\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\|\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))}^{2}.

Using that ‖φδ‖Hk​(𝕋d)≤Cδk+d/2\|\varphi_{\delta}\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{d})}\leq\frac{C}{\delta^{k+d/2}} we finally obtain

∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε​(t+h,⋅)∗φδ​(x)−fε​(t,⋅)∗φδ​(x)|2​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t≤C​T​hδk+d/2​‖∂tfε​(s,⋅)‖L2​(0,T,H−k​(𝕋d))2.\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)\ast\varphi_{\delta}(x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq CT\frac{h}{{\delta^{k+d/2}}}\,\|\partial_{t}f_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-k}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))}^{2}.

Now, if fε​(t,x)f_{\varepsilon}(t,x) is not smooth in time, we extend it with fε​(0,x)f_{\varepsilon}(0,x) for t<0t<0, fε​(T,x)f_{\varepsilon}(T,x) for t>Tt>T and apply usual regularization to obtain the same estimate. Hence, if we choose h⁡(δ)=δ2​k+dh(\delta)=\delta^{2k+d} we conclude

limh→0lim supε→0∫0T−h∫𝕋d|fε​(t+h,x)−fε​(t,x)|2​⁡d​x​⁡𝑑t≤θ⁡(h).\lim_{h\to 0}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T-h}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|f_{\varepsilon}(t+h,x)-f_{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\leq\theta(h).

Combined with the compactness in space (B.5) and the Fréchet-Kolmogorov theorem we obtain the compactness of {fε}\{f_{\varepsilon}\} in L2​((0,T)×𝕋d)L^{2}((0,T)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}). ∎
